title: France Votes a Data Traffic Tax on Google and Meta, 10 Billion Euros Expected
summary: France votes data traffic tax on Google and Meta expecting 10 billion euros
detailed: The National Assembly is the lower house of the Paris Parliament, and the budget bill (in French the projet de loi de finances , or PLF) goes through it on first reading before heading to the Senate.

sentences: The National Assembly is the lower house of the Paris Parliament, and the budget bill (in French the projet de loi de finances , or PLF) goes through it on first reading before heading to the Senate.
An amendment is a change proposed by individual deputies or by a group.
This one carries the number I-1358 and the signature of Laurent Lhardit with the Socialist group.
A similar version had been rejected on October 9 in the finance committee , then returned to the floor and passed on October 30.
In the text filed with the Assembly , the new levy is called the " taxe sur les producteurs de données numériques ".

The operators (Orange, SFR, Bouygues Telecom and Free, according to the French press) would have to prepare a consolidated, anonymous count of the data directed at their customers, with the sender's name, its registration number with IANA (the body that assigns internet addresses and network numbers) and the quantity transmitted.
Nothing is recorded about content or destination.
The count goes up every three months to the DGFiP, the French public finance directorate, in other words the tax office, under the supervision of Arcep (the national communications authority).
A special rule covers CDNs, the content delivery networks, which are servers that keep copies of sites and videos close to users so they arrive faster.
When a sender goes through a CDN, the taxed volume is the sum of the flows leaving the CDN.

In its statement of reasons, the amendment names Google, Meta, Amazon, Netflix and Akamai (an American cloud and CDN group), which together account for roughly half the traffic measured by Arcep, estimated at 200 billion gigabytes a year.
The levy has a ceiling, 15% of revenue earned in France or 2% of worldwide revenue, designed for sectors that move many gigabytes for every euro collected, such as video on demand and video games.
The base is, in effect, delivery to French citizens, not where the company is headquartered.

Groups with a company in France would pay under the same rules as corporate tax, while those without a subsidiary would get a notice from the tax office by January 30 and have to pay in euros by March 30 of the year after the measurement.
The signatories pitch it as a base that cannot be moved, unlike the profits digital groups book in whichever country they prefer.
According to the French press the tax would also hit YouTube, TikTok and even television networks, and Lhardit cited TF1, for which he estimates a bill of 200,000 to 300,000 euros a year.
Multiplying Arcep's 200 billion gigabytes by 0.055 euros gives about 11 billion gross, before the caps (the 15% and 2% limits on revenue).
Universfreebox, by contrast, headlines a maximum of 5 billion.
Public Accounts Minister David Amiel said about half the revenue would fall on smaller providers, French ones included, according to KultureGeek's account .
Five Socialist deputies said yes, along with 2 from La France insoumise, 2 Greens and 2 from the democratic and republican left group, 11 in all, against 10 opposed.
The government had, after all, recommended against it, as did the general rapporteur of the finance committee, who fears the costs would be passed on to advertisers, KultureGeek reports again.
The budget bill now has to finish its first reading in the Assembly and then go to the Senate.
There is also a faster route to wiping out the amendment.

Article 49, paragraph 3, of the French Constitution lets the government have a text adopted without a vote unless a no-confidence motion passes, and in that case the executive could pick a version without the tax.
Universfreebox also warns the text could be modified or struck before final adoption.
Behind the French detail sits a methodological choice that matters to anyone watching how platforms are taxed.
So far Europe taxes digital multinationals on revenue, with France, Italy and Spain applying a 3% levy (in Italy above 750 million euros of worldwide revenue) and the United Kingdom 2%.
Here the base becomes the weight of the data delivered, a number no accounting engineering can shift elsewhere.
In October 2025 French deputies had already voted to double the revenue tax from 3% to 6%.
In 2019 the US administration opened a trade investigation (Section 301) into the first version of the same levy.
The risk, however, is that the gigabyte becomes a pricing lever.
A traffic tax rewards efficiency (the signatories say so openly in the amendment, with less data and better compression), but it weighs more on those who sell video and games.
For a group like Meta, which already faces pressure from publishers in Europe (see the Norwegian media lawsuit in Oslo ), a second tax front would be one more problem.

Network operators have asked for years that platforms contribute to network costs (in Brussels the debate goes by the name "fair share"), and here the request arrives from another direction, the tax office.
A Friday vote with 21 votes cast, and a 10 billion bill that another French outlet cuts in half.
If the tax survives the Senate and Article 49.3, the debate will resume with a real text in hand.
Until then it remains a political signal, the kind other countries' tax offices copy faster than they copy laws.
The text does not provide for it, but the risk exists.
The tax falls on the sender of the data, which could, however, pass it on to prices, subscriptions or advertisers.

Telesatellite calculates a theoretical cost of 30.53 euros gross for a household using 555 GB a month, falling to about 20 euros with the cap for Netflix, while a user quoted by Universfreebox guesses 27.50 euros on 500 GB.
These are scenarios, and no provider has decided anything.
The amendment gives no entry-into-force date, since the Senate, the outcome on Article 49.3 and promulgation all come first.
For foreign groups the calendar provides for measurement over one year, the tax office notice by January 30 and payment by March 30 of the following year.
The French 3% tax applies to groups with more than 750 million euros in worldwide revenue and 25 million in France, and measures a share of turnover.
This one counts gigabytes delivered, so a low-margin, high-traffic service would pay more, which is why the revenue cap exists.
